paragraphs.text: This [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) was made in Guangxi in the 1990s and packed loose into a small bamboo basket lined with bamboo leaves, the old [basket packing](liu-bao:making-traditional) of the tea. Like every [dark tea](dark:definition), its leaf was heaped after it was made so that warmth, moisture and microbes could darken and soften it, and then it was left to age. This lot did its ageing in humid storage in Hong Kong, over many years.

Most Liu Bao of this age is [old stock](liu-bao:old-stock) that sat in warehouses in Malaysia or Hong Kong after the tin mining trade ended, and the place where it was kept gives each lot its own character. Made in the 1990s, it is well past the ten the trade needs before it calls a Liu Bao [aged](liu-bao:age-aged), and how it was stored counts for as much as how long.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
